pagetitle: "Where the back-ends differ"

# Where the back-ends differ

Four back-ends ship: LaTeX (and the PDF it typesets), HTML, EPUB and Typst. The
marking syntax means the same thing in all of them. What the indexes can do
differs, because the tools underneath them do.

EPUB and HTML build the same index out of the same document nodes, so every
row below that says "in HTML" is true of EPUB too. The two places EPUB parts
company with HTML — a book is one Pandoc process there, and its locators are
sequence numbers with no pages behind them — are on the [EPUB](epub.qmd) page.
Typst orders and groups its entries the way HTML does and prints them with page
numbers; the [Typst](typst.qmd) page describes it.

1. **No level ceiling in HTML or Typst.** Sub-entries nest as deep as you
   write them. The three-level ceiling described on [Sub-entry
   levels](sub-entry-levels.qmd) is `makeindex`'s limit, not the
   extension's.
2. **The one-entry warning is LaTeX-only.** A term marked two different ways
   reaches the LaTeX index tool as one entry the extension had to compose, so
   the extension says it did. An HTML or Typst index prints the locator and the
   cross-reference together on one entry by itself, with nothing to compose,
   so the warning would name a decision that format never has to make.
3. **Sorting is the extension's own in HTML and Typst.** Top-level entries are
   ranked into letter groups first; inside a group, and at every level below
   the top, the order folds ASCII uppercase to lowercase and then compares
   character codes, breaking a tie by character code, over an entry's sort key
   where it has one. In LaTeX the order is `makeindex`'s. Neither collates
   accented or non-Latin text the way a language would, which is what sort
   keys are for.
4. **Locators are numbered links in HTML**, in the order the marks are
   written, where LaTeX gives page numbers. Typst gives page numbers too, in
   page order, and each one links to its page.
5. **Cross-reference targets are hyperlinked in HTML** when the target names an
   entry in the same index, and are plain text otherwise. In the LaTeX and
   Typst indexes a target is always plain text.
6. **A cross-reference carries no locator in any of the four back-ends.** The
   `see also` limitation described on [Cross-references](cross-references.qmd)
   is the same in all of them.
7. **The principal mention is emphasized everywhere**, but by different means:
   the LaTeX back-end wraps the page number in a command you can redefine, the
   HTML back-end marks the link with a class and a `<strong>`, and the Typst
   back-end sets the page number in bold.
8. **A page range is a page range only in LaTeX and Typst.** `makeindex` prints
   one span of pages, `12--15`, and so does Typst, `12–15`; HTML has no pages,
   so a range there is one numbered link at the opening mark. Each back-end
   prints one locator where you wrote two marks, which is what the syntax
   means. Typst
   prints only the ranges you write: marks on pages 3, 4 and 5 print
   `3, 4, 5`, where `makeindex` folds three or more pages in a row into a
   range.
9. **The extension's own words are settable in HTML, EPUB and Typst, and its
   punctuation in HTML and EPUB.** The `Symbols` group heading, the `see` and
   `see also` in front of a cross-reference, and the punctuation inside an
   entry are the extension's rather than yours, and `index-labels:` — keys
   `symbols`, `see`, `see-also`, `separator` and `xref-separator`, written at a
   document's top level or inside one `indexes:` entry, the nearer setting
   winning key by key — sets them for the HTML and EPUB indexes. The Typst
   index reads the three word keys and neither separator key: it always prints
   a comma before a locator and a semicolon between two cross-references.
   `index-labels:` reaches the LaTeX back-end nowhere:
   that one emits `\see` and `\seealso`, whose two words babel supplies from
   your document's `lang:`. There is no third word to set there — a LaTeX index
   has no letter groups at all, so it prints no `Symbols` heading for
   `symbols:` to override. Neither separator key reaches it either: what stands
   between a term and its page numbers there is `makeindex`'s own delimiter,
   and what stands between two cross-references is written into the LaTeX this
   extension emits — in two places, the command it defines for a term carrying
   both kinds and the join it writes when a term's targets ride the
   encapsulation channel instead.
10. **All four back-ends follow `lang:`, and share nothing else about it.**
    Every back-end picks its own words from your document's language, and
    that language is the whole of what they have in common: LaTeX asks babel,
    HTML, EPUB and Typst read a table this extension ships. Two consequences
    follow. The languages covered are not the same — babel covers hundreds,
    this extension covers Spanish, French, German and Italian, and German only
    in part, so a document in a language babel knows and this table does not
    gets a localized LaTeX PDF and an English HTML, EPUB or Typst index. And
    `index-labels:` is read by the HTML, EPUB and Typst back-ends alone, so a
    word you set there changes those indexes and never the LaTeX PDF, where
    babel's word stands. Setting a word for all four means writing
    `index-labels:` for HTML, EPUB and Typst and redefining `\seename` or
    `\alsoname` for LaTeX.
